verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Mundra edible-oil processors with proven throughput and tight stock controls; avoid thinly capitalised vanaspati units and any borrower whose working-capital book is growing faster than volumes.
title: Mundra Edible Oils & Vanaspati: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**Crushing, refining and packing oil is a throughput business, not a margin business.** You buy seed or crude oil, crush or refine it, and sell meal, refined oil and vanaspati into a market where your price is set by the commodity, not by you. Peer evidence is blunt: AWL Agri grew revenue 22% to Rs 17,605 crore in Q2FY26 while EBIT fell 13% to Rs 502 crore [1]. **Volume and working-capital turns make the money; price does not.**

## Where cash sits and what has changed
**Cash is trapped in inventory and receivables, and the inventory is a moving price.** Raw-material cost is the largest cost line for these businesses [5], and edible-oil companies carry direct risk from raw-material price volatility [7]. Margins are thin and competition is fragmented, with PBILDT margins of 1.47% to 3.32% seen at a vanaspati peer [6]. **So when a proposal lands, check stock days and whether the drawing power is built on today's oil price or last quarter's; if the borrower values stock at the higher of the two, ask for the valuation policy in writing.**

## The growth opportunity in Mundra
**Gujarat is running ahead of India on collections, +11.9% Apr-to-date against +6.1% nationally [D], so the local trade is moving.** Peer results show where the volume is: AWL's Q4 revenue rose 18% to Rs 21,465 crore on 14% volume growth, with operational EBITDA up 40% to Rs 628 crore [2][3]. **Pursue refiners and packers with own throughput, branded or institutional offtake, and a track record of holding margin per MT through a price swing.** Avoid pure traders with no plant, and vanaspati units with no brand and no distribution. **Note the sources say nothing specific about Mundra itself; this is first principles plus peers.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the commodity, not the balance sheet.** Sanction working capital against a stock-and-receivables statement, with a margin that holds when oil prices fall. Take monthly stock statements, monthly sales and volume data, and quarterly CMA. **If bank credit nationally is growing +45.5% YoY against output of +5.1% [D], then a borrower whose own book grows far faster than its volumes is borrowing against price, not production; ask for the volume reconciliation.** Exports are down 26.0% Apr-to-date in USD [D], so do not underwrite a new export-led line without a confirmed buyer.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch stock days, not just overdue.** A rise in inventory days while volumes are flat means the borrower is holding a falling price. **If stock days rise two months running, cut drawing power and ask for the ageing.** Watch for interest-payment delays even of a day: a large peer had a one-day technical delay on a working-capital demand loan interest of about Rs 65 lakh [8]. **If a payment slips, treat it as a cash-flow signal and re-price or exit.**
watch: Stock days rise two months running -> cut drawing power and seek stock ageing
Book grows faster than volumes -> ask for volume reconciliation and re-size limit
Any delay, even one day -> treat as cash-flow signal, re-price or exit
Sharp fall in oil price -> revalue stock and test margin cushion
Export share rising without confirmed buyers -> decline new export-led limits
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
